extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, college-algebra instructors, curriculum/textbook designers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and evaluation of worked examples in college algebra textbooks (community-college context), using frameworks for cognitive demand, control-of-work, representations, and response types to judge how well examples support student learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental research design for instructional activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional activities should (a) link up with the informal situated knowledge of the students, (b) enable them to develop more sophisticated, abstract, formal knowledge, and (c) comply with the basic principle of intellectual autonomy (Gravemeijer, 1998).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use developmental research to design tasks that start from students' informal knowledge and guide reinvention toward formal concepts while preserving students' intellectual autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided reinvention heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: A process by which students formalize their informal understandings and intuitions (Gravemeijer et al., 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that prompt students to reconstruct mathematical definitions/ideas (e.g., asking them to complete 'A series converges when...'), iteratively refine their definitions, and unpack meanings of elements (N, error bounds, quantifiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional objective: students generate rigorous definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Central objective of the teaching experiment: for students to generate rigorous definitions of sequence convergence, series convergence, and pointwise convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success can be evaluated by whether students produce definitions capturing formal quantifier structure and roles of N and error bounds, and whether they can unpack components across contexts (sequences → series → pointwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide graphical references in instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students to produce graphs of series and Taylor polynomials to provide reference points for constructing definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical artifacts helped students refer back while constructing definitions; instructors' prompting to produce/interpret graphs supported reinvention of formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage prior definitions across topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use students' prior activity (e.g., defining sequence convergence) to support later definitions (series convergence, pointwise convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly prompt students to reinterpret sequence-definition elements (N, error bounds, quantifiers) for series and Taylor series contexts to scaffold transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use approximation terminology to support interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and use approximation-frame terminology (approximations, error, error bounds) to help students interpret components of formal definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent use of approximation language (error bounds, N) aids meaningful interpretation of definitions and helps students see connections among definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Demand — Memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: A category in the Cognitive Demand framework (Stein et al., 2000) representing tasks that require recall or reproduction of facts or procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memorization is lowest complexity; desirable curricula should have few or no memorization examples (the study found 0% memorization examples across analyzed texts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Demand — Procedures Without Connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks that ask students to carry out a procedure but do not require them to make connections to underlying concepts (Stein et al., 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the dominant category in the corpus (≈90%). While practicing procedures is valuable, overreliance limits students' perception of what mathematics is; aim to reduce the proportion in favor of higher-demand tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Demand — Procedures With Connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks where students not only perform procedures but also make connections to underlying concepts or representations (Stein et al., 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked as more conceptually rich (10% in study); include more tasks that require linking procedures to concepts to foster deeper understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Demand — Doing Mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: High-demand, open-ended tasks that require problem formulation, analysis, conjecture, or exploration (Stein et al., 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare in the corpus (1%); increasing such tasks supports students' capacity to think and reason mathematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling the Work — Further Elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: An aspect of the 'Controlling the Work' framework examining whether solutions provide additional elaboration that helps students control their work (Mesa, 2010).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 9% of examples provided further elaboration. Including elaboration helps learners understand solution structure and strategies for verifying their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling the Work — Correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether solutions explicitly address correctness (e.g., checks or indicators that the solution is correct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only 9% of examples in the corpus modeled checking correctness; textbooks should include explicit correctness strategies to teach students how to verify answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling the Work — Suggestion to Check
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the example or solution suggests checks or ways to validate intermediate steps or final answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very rare in the corpus (2%). Suggesting checks trains students to monitor and control their problem-solving process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling the Work — Plausibility or Interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work includes plausibility checks or interpretation of results (e.g., does the answer make sense in context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices that encourage interpretation are absent (0% in corpus); including plausibility checks fosters deeper understanding and error detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Representation — Symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of symbolic representations (algebraic notation, formulas) in example statements and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols were most frequent in example statements (73%); encourage balanced use across statements and solutions and connections to other representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Representation — Tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of tabular/numeric-array representations in statements and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables were infrequent in statements (5%) and solutions (12%); using tables can support pattern recognition and multiple-representation fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Representation — Graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphical representations (plots, sketches) used in example statements and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphs appeared in 10% of statements and 37% of solutions; using graphs more often and linking them to symbolic work supports multiple-representation skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Representation — Numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric or computational representations (specific numbers, computations) in statements and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers were common in statements (31%) and most frequent in solutions (71%); avoid overreliance on rote numeric examples—connect numbers back to conceptual ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Representation — Verbal
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal/written descriptions or explanations used as representations in examples and solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbal representations appeared less frequently (20% statements, 9% solutions); including verbal explanations supports sense-making and justification skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Response — Only Answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Example expects only a final answer with no mathematical sentence or justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 46% of examples expected only answer responses. Overuse limits opportunities for revealing student reasoning; reduce Only Answer items in favor of justificatory responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Response — Answer and Mathematical Sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Example expects a final answer plus a brief mathematical sentence (short justificatory statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less common than Only Answer; valuable for eliciting succinct reasoning alongside answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Response — Answer and Graph
rubrics_metrics.description: Example expects a numeric/analytic answer and an accompanying graph as part of the response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All textbooks had more Answer-and-Graph responses than Answer-and-Mathematical-Sentence; use such items to connect analytic and visual reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Response — Explanation or Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Example expects students to provide explanation or reasoning supporting their answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatively rare (0%–15% across textbooks); increasing these items helps uncover misconceptions and develop justificatory competence in students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Response — Making a Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Example asks students to make a choice (e.g., select which method or representation is appropriate) and justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare across textbooks (0%–6%); useful for fostering metacognitive and decision-making skills in problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability for coding
rubrics_metrics.description: The inter-rater reliability between two coders ranged from 74% to 96% across analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using these coding frameworks, report coder agreement; acceptable reliability strengthens claims about textbook characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative criterion: examples should model strategies for controlling the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook examples should explicitly show strategies to control work (elaboration, correctness checks, suggestions to check, plausibility/interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study argues that lack of explicit control strategies reduces students' opportunities to learn to use these strategies; authors/instructors should add these elements to examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative criterion: favor tasks that require explanation and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples should ask for explanations or justifications rather than only final answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asking for explanations helps teachers and students uncover misconceptions and supports development of mathematical argumentation; increase frequency of these tasks in textbooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative criterion: promote multiple representations and connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples should include and connect symbolic, numeric, graphical, tabular, and verbal representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low percentages of tables, graphs, and verbal representations suggest few cross-representational connections; encourage problems that require generating and translating among representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note on real-world/technology contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of real-world contexts or technology does not guarantee high cognitive demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not assume context/technology implies reform-oriented high-demand tasks; explicitly design the task's cognitive complexity regardless of context.
